title: Pauli Ring
experiment: Parity effect: an even number of fermions on a ring prefers half a flux quantum (Leggett)
intro: Two identical fermions on one ring, at rest on opposite sides. This level measures both momenta at once (across: k₁, down: k₂), and the target is the small cold square |k₁|, |k₂| < 0.1, where both are nearly at rest. On a ring only one allowed momentum, k = 0, fits inside it, and two fermions cannot both have it. Find the flux that makes room for both.
goal: Set the flux Φ through the ring so that both fermions are found in the cold square (both momenta below 0.1). Without a flux the only allowed momentum there is 0, and the exclusion principle forbids both having it.

physics.point: Two fermions need two different momenta. Without a flux the cold square holds only k = 0; half a flux quantum shifts the comb to ±π/L, two teeth inside it, one for each fermion. An even number of fermions on a ring prefers half a flux quantum.

idea: The exclusion principle says two identical fermions never share a state. On a ring the states are the teeth of the momentum comb, so two fermions at rest cannot both have k = 0: one has to move. That costs energy, unless the comb itself shifts.

With half a flux quantum the comb is k = (2n + 1)π/L, symmetric about zero with no tooth at zero: the two lowest states are ±π/L, one for each fermion, and the pair is cold again. Leggett pointed out (1991) that this makes the ground state of a ring hold an even number of fermions most comfortably at half a flux quantum, and an odd number at zero: a parity effect seen in persistent currents of small metal rings. Twisting the boundary by π is the same as making the fermions' wave function antiperiodic.
Bosons have no such problem: both can sit at k = 0, and without a flux they fill the cold square.
maths: The launch is two wide packets (σ = 8, wider than half the ring, so each is summed over its periodic images; that puts 92% of its momentum on the single tooth k = 0 without a flux, or on ±π/L with half a quantum) at x = 10 and x = 30, antisymmetrised: ψ(x₁, x₂) = g(x₁ − 10) g(x₂ − 30) − g(x₂ − 10) g(x₁ − 30). In momentum space this vanishes on the diagonal k₁ = k₂, and is largest where (k₁ − k₂)·20 = π, exactly the pair ±π/L for L = 40.
The target is |k₁|, |k₂| < 0.1 with sharp edges; the comb spacing is 2π/40 ≈ 0.157. Measured:
With both particles threaded, a whole comb tooth of each needs a whole flux quantum, so the fermions' response repeats every Φ₀.
try: Flux 0: the momentum view shows a grid of allowed (k₁, k₂) with the diagonal empty; the cold square holds only (0, 0), which is on it.
Flux 0.5: the grid slides by half a tooth, and the points (−π/L, +π/L) and (+π/L, −π/L) land in the square, off the diagonal.
Compare with 9-4: there the flux shifted the total momentum; here it is the individual momenta that matter.
